title: A boy's lunch (John 6:1–14)
hook: five loaves and two fish from a child, and five thousand eat with baskets left over

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Samaritan woman at a well, and a long talk at noon about living water.

Not enough money for the month. Not enough time. Not enough patience for the kids tonight. Some sums never add up. Here's one on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has followed Jesus there, because they've seen him heal the sick. Thousands of them, and nothing to eat. Jesus turns to one of his disciples, Philip, and asks a question John says was a test: where are we going to buy bread for all these people?
screen: `OBVIOUSLY NOT ENOUGH.` → `A HUNGRY CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.` → `WHERE SHALL WE BUY BREAD?`

segments.voice: Philip does the math, in the King James Bible: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." A penny there is a denarius, a laborer's day's wage in one of Jesus's parables: two hundred days' wages, and still not a bite each. Then Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, comes back with something almost funny: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Only John mentions the boy. Barley, some readers point out, was the cheaper grain. This is a kid's packed lunch, and somebody has to hand it over. Jesus has the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men, John says. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Then a quieter line: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Twelve, from five loaves. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell this feeding too; it's in all four Gospels. Christians read it as a wonder, and some also hear in it the table of communion: he takes bread, gives thanks, and gives it. Later in the chapter he calls himself the bread of life. But start with the boy. Nobody asks him to fix the problem. He offers what he has, small as it is, and it turns out to be enough, with baskets to spare.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED DAYS' WAGES, NOT ENOUGH.` · `FIVE BARLEY LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `HE GIVES THANKS AND GIVES.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.` · then, large: `THAT NOTHING BE LOST.`

segments.voice: Think of a need you know about right now, a struggling friend, a cause you care about, a tired colleague, a lonely family member. Instead of everything it would take, look at what you actually have, ten minutes, a skill, a spare meal, a kind word, your five loaves and two fish, and picture handing it over. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first, the way he did.
Fragments. The broken pieces gathered up after the crowd ate their fill, twelve baskets of them, so that nothing from five loaves and two fish would be lost.
Your line: it was enough. Five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets left over. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many churches read the feeding of the five thousand alongside teaching about communion and about sharing with people in need. Some church meals and food programs point to this story.

what it means: a child hands over a small lunch, it's given thanks for and given away, and it turns out to be enough.
what a scholar hears: barley was the cheaper grain, and the words took, gave thanks, gave echo the Last Supper, which is why some Christians hear communion in this meal.

notes: Denarius as a day's wage (Matthew 20:2); two hundred denarii as 'more than half a year's pay'. Confirm.
'The only miracle, apart from the resurrection, told in all four Gospels' — commonly stated; confirm.
Barley as the cheaper grain, bread of the poor; commonly stated; confirm.
'About five thousand men' (John 6:10); the script does not estimate women and children.

The Eucharistic echo (took, gave thanks, distributed; John 6:11 uses eucharistesas) is presented as how many Christians hear it, not as the only reading. The script does not mention the modern 'sharing' reading of the miracle.

Second review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'You know that moment ... Now picture'; 'it's getting late, no town, no market' (from the other Gospels, not John) cut; 'more than half a year's pay' now the text's own two hundred pence, with the day's wage cited to Matthew 20:2; barley-as-poor-bread attributed ('some readers'); 'the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell' (voice and myth) cut as an unsourced superlative; 'Christians have always' and 'many' softened; stock 'a line people skip past' and the food-bank generalization replaced.
